Régine Alexandra Chassagne was born in [Montreal](/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), [Quebec](/wiki/Quebec "Quebec"), Canada, and grew up in [St-Lambert](/wiki/Saint-Lambert,_Quebec "Saint-Lambert, Quebec"), a suburb south of Montreal.[[2]](#cite_note-Mirror-2)[[3]](#cite_note-RTÉ-3) Her parents, who were Haitians of mixed French and African descent, moved from Haiti during the dictatorship of [François Duvalier](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), which is alluded to in the Arcade Fire song "Haïti", in which she sings, **Mes cousins jamais nés hantent les nuits de Duvalier** ("My unborn cousins haunt Duvalier's nights").[[4]](#cite_note-4) The line is in reference to the relatives who were killed during the [Jérémie Vespers](/wiki/J%C3%A9r%C3%A9mie_Vespers "Jérémie Vespers") massacre.

Chassagne attended *[Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf](/wiki/Coll%C3%A8ge_Jean-de-Br%C3%A9beuf "Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf")* before earning a B.A. in communication studies at [Concordia University](/wiki/Concordia_University_(Montreal) "Concordia University (Montreal)")[[5]](#cite_note-5) in 1998,[[6]](#cite_note-6) and went on to study jazz voice briefly at [McGill University](/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University").[[7]](#cite_note-7) She was singing jazz at an art opening at Concordia in 2000, when Win Butler met her and persuaded her to join his band.

Chassagne has also been involved with a medieval-themed band called *Les Jongleurs de la Mandragore*[[8]](#cite_note-8) and with Jimmy Rouleau in the jazz duo Azúcar.[[9]](#cite_note-9) She also wrote the music for the two-minute [David Uloth](/wiki/David_Uloth "David Uloth") short film "The Shine", and she contributed to the UNICEF benefit project as part of the North American Hallowe'en Prevention Initiative, performing the song "[Do They Know It's Hallowe'en?](/wiki/Do_They_Know_It%27s_Hallowe%27en%3F "Do They Know It's Hallowe'en?")" along with Win Butler.

Wright brothers at their Dayton, Ohio, home in 1909

The [Wright Company](/wiki/Wright_Company "Wright Company") was incorporated on November 22, 1909. The brothers sold their patents to the company for $100,000 and also received one-third of the shares in a million dollar stock issue and a 10 percent royalty on every airplane sold.[[154]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouch2003410-162) With Wilbur as president and Orville as vice president, the company set up a factory in Dayton and a [flying school](/wiki/Wright_Flying_School "Wright Flying School") / test flight field at Huffman Prairie; the headquarters office was in New York City.

In mid-1910, the Wrights changed the design of the *Wright Flyer*, moving the horizontal elevator from the front to the back and adding wheels although keeping the skids as part of the undercarriage unit. It had become apparent by then that a rear elevator would make an airplane easier to control, especially as higher speeds grew more common. The new version was designated the "Model B", although the original canard design was never referred to as the "Model A" by the Wrights. However, the U.S. Army Signal Corps which bought the airplane did call it "Wright type A".[[155]](#cite_note-163)

There were not many customers for airplanes, so in early 1910 the Wrights hired and trained the [Wright Exhibition Team](/wiki/Wright_Exhibition_Team "Wright Exhibition Team") of salaried pilots to show off their machines and win prize money for the company – despite Wilbur's disdain for what he called "the [mountebank](/wiki/Charlatan "Charlatan") business". A bilingual parking sign in Nuuk in Danish and Greenlandic

[Greenlandic](/wiki/Greenlandic_language "Greenlandic language") (effectively [West Greenlandic](/wiki/West_Greenlandic "West Greenlandic")), spoken by nearly 50,000 people, became the sole official language in 2009.[[212]](#cite_note-219) The majority of the population speak both [Danish](/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language") and West Greenlandic Kalaallisut (the most populous [Eskaleut language](/wiki/Eskaleut_language "Eskaleut language")). They have been used in public affairs since the establishment of home rule in 1979. In practice, Danish is still widely used in administration, academia, and skilled trades and other professions. The orthography of Greenlandic, established in 1851,[[213]](#cite_note-220) was [revised](/wiki/Kalaallisut_orthography "Kalaallisut orthography") in 1973. The [literacy rate](/wiki/Literacy "Literacy") was 100% in 2007.[[186]](#cite_note-cia-factbook-193)

About 12% of the population speak Danish as their primary language. These are primarily Danish immigrants, many of whom speak Danish as their first and sometimes only language. Monolingual Danish speakers are concentrated in Nuuk and other larger towns. A debate about the roles of Greenlandic and Danish in the country's future is ongoing. While Greenlandic was dominant in all smaller settlements, most of the multi-ethnic Inuit ancestors spoke Danish as a second language. In larger towns, especially Nuuk, Danish was more important for social matters. English is growing in importance, and is now taught from the first school year.[[214]](#cite_note-221)

Some individuals attain much greater diameter; the largest known being "The Bulga Stump", a charred remnant near Tarra Bulga, South [Gippsland](/wiki/Gippsland "Gippsland") district, [Victoria, Australia](/wiki/Victoria,_Australia "Victoria, Australia") which as a living tree had a DBH of 10.77 metres (35 ft 4 in),[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51) making *E. regnans* the third thickest species of tree after the Baobab (*[Adansonia digitata](/wiki/Adansonia_digitata "Adansonia digitata")*) and the Montezuma Cypress (*[Taxodium mucronatum](/wiki/Taxodium_mucronatum "Taxodium mucronatum")*). As a consequence of being both the tallest and thickest Australian trees, *E. regnans* is also the most massive; that title being currently held by an individual called the "Kermandie Queen" discovered 3.9 kilometres (2.4 mi) west of [Geeveston](/wiki/Geeveston "Geeveston"), [Tasmania](/wiki/Tasmania "Tasmania") which measures 76.99 metres (252 ft 7 in) in height and has a diameter at breast height (DBH) of 6.88 metres (22 ft 7 in).[[52]](#cite_note-52)

Al Carder notes that in 1888 a cash reward of 100 pounds was offered there for the discovery of any tree measuring more than 400 feet (120 m).[[48]](#cite_note-Carder-48) The fact that such a considerable reward was never claimed is taken as evidence that such large trees did not exist. Carder's historical research, however, revealed that the reward was offered under conditions that made it highly unlikely to be collected. First, it was made in the depths of winter and applied only for a very short time. Next, the tree had to be measured by an accredited surveyor.
